title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

errors: No arithmetical errors on this page. The node sum is −66"+826"+61" = +821" = 13'41", giving 92°34'24"; the inclination is 5°16'59.5" − 5" = 5°16'54.5", rounded to 5°16'54"; the averaged mid-time is ≈13h56'3", rounded to 13h56'0".

On the preceding page the perturbed coefficient 2435.166/2133.633 computes to ≈1.1413, not the printed 1.14105 (possibly a misprint or transcription issue). This barely affects Euler's 5" conclusion here.

ideas.what: Sensitivity (error-propagation) argument: a coefficient that is homogeneous of degree 0 in the dominant uncertain quantity n is robust to errors in n, whereas formulas not homogeneous in n require true hourly motions
ideas.modern_name: qualitative error propagation / sensitivity analysis via homogeneity
ideas.usually_credited_to: informal practice of 18th-c. astronomers (Euler, Mayer, Lambert); systematic treatment later (Gauss, Laplace)
ideas.where_published: Euler discusses tolerable errors in many astronomical papers; no specific location for this argument

ideas.what: Determining true node and inclination from mid-eclipse timings of a total lunar eclipse, using averages of contact times and the equation of time
ideas.modern_name: eclipse reduction for lunar orbital elements
ideas.where_published: Euler's lunar works (E187 Theoria motus lunae, 1753; lunar tables) treat eclipses; this specific chapter appears only in the Opera postuma

ideas.what: Tabular node equations and inclination variation depending on the node−Sun elongation (≈13'46" here; inclination 5°17' varying)
ideas.modern_name: Tycho's inequalities of the node and inclination (evection-type solar terms)
ideas.where_published: Euler's lunar tables (e.g. within E187 and his 1746 tables)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computational page: closing remarks on error tolerance plus a standard reduction of the 1722 eclipse with tabular node and inclination values. The arithmetic is correct and nothing in it is novel or unrecognized.
